imageCaption: Battle of Jena-Auerstedt, October 14, 1806. Napoleon's double envelopment destroyed Prussian strategic confidence in a single day. The Prussian army, believed to be one of Europe's strongest, ceased to exist as a cohesive force.

longForm.title: Jena-Auerstedt: The Myth of Prussian Military Excellence
longForm.excerpt: On October 14, 1806, Napoleon defeated the Prussian army at Jena and simultaneously defeated another Prussian column at Auerstedt. The Prussian strategy was based on false assumptions about French strength and Prussian defensive capabilities. By nightfall, the Prussian army was shattered. Prussia lost the war before it properly began.
paragraphs: The Prussian decision to enter the War of the Fourth Coalition on October 9, 1806, was predicated on a strategic miscalculation of measurable dimensions. The Prussian General Staff estimated French strength at 170,000 men. French First Army strength, under Napoleon's command, was closer to 210,000. The Prussian estimate of their own army's capability, meanwhile, was based on the assumption that Prussian defensive doctrine—linear formations with musket fire and disciplined retreat—would neutralize French column tactics. This assumption had not been tested since 1792. In the interim, the French Army had fought twelve years of continuous warfare. Prussian officers had fought one campaign: the War of the First Coalition in 1792–1793, during which Prussia had been part of a coalition and had not directly faced Napoleon's maneuver warfare. The Prussian assumption was not that they were stronger than France, but that their strategic position—fighting on interior lines with support from Russian forces moving westward—would allow them to defend until Russian strength arrived. The mathematics of this strategy required that the Prussian army maintain its force integrity long enough to coordinate with Russian columns. The strategy was logical. The assumption that the Prussian army could survive a direct encounter with Napoleon was not.

Napoleon's advance from the Rhine in early October 1806 was designed to prevent Prussian-Russian coordination. The French army would move northwest at speed, drive a wedge between Prussian and Russian forces, and defeat them in detail. The Prussian command structure initially recognized the threat. Prussia's main army under Prince Hohenlohe was positioned near Jena. A second column, the Royal Prussian Army under the Duke of Brunswick, was positioned northeast near Auerstedt. The distance between the two forces was 30 kilometers. The Prussian plan was to concentrate these forces, move north, and engage the French. The execution collapsed immediately. Communication between the two Prussian commanders was poor. Reconnaissance reports understated French strength and overstated the speed of Russian movement. By October 13, the two Prussian columns had not concentrated. Napoleon had moved faster than Prussian planning anticipated. The French were between the two Prussian armies, not where the Prussian General Staff had positioned them in operational maps.

On October 14, 1806, Napoleon attacked the Prussian main force at Jena with 96,000 men against 54,000 Prussians under Hohenlohe. Simultaneously, at Auerstedt, 27 kilometers away, 27,500 French troops under Marshal Davout engaged 63,000 Prussians under Brunswick. The tactical situation at Jena strongly favored the Prussian defender: the terrain offered good defensive positions. Hohenlohe's forces held a ridge line. The battle opened with Prussian artillery fire that inflicted casualties on advancing French columns. The Prussian General Staff had been confident in artillery superiority. What Prussian analysis had not fully credited was the French system of artillery massing: concentrating gun batteries to create local fire superiority at the point of attack. By mid-morning at Jena, the Prussian ridge line had come under concentrated French artillery bombardment. Infantry assault followed. The Prussian line, attacked frontally while being subjected to artillery fire and threatened with envelopment, began to collapse.

The critical failure at Jena was a command decision: Hohenlohe did not commit his reserves. The Prussian doctrine called for the holding of a reserve force for counterattack after the enemy assault had been repelled. Hohenlohe had held 20,000 men in reserve, based on this doctrine. The attack was not repelled. As the Prussian line deteriorated, Hohenlohe chose to retreat rather than commit the reserves. The reasoning, Hohenlohe later stated, was that he believed his reserves would be necessary to cover the retreat. This decision was logical given the assumption that the battle was lost. It was tactically sound. It was strategically catastrophic because it eliminated any possibility of a fighting withdrawal that might preserve the army's force structure. The reserve was instead used to screen retreat. By 1400 hours, the Prussian main army at Jena was in full retreat.

At Auerstedt, meanwhile, the tactical situation was reversed. Davout, with 27,500 men, faced 63,000 Prussians under Brunswick. Standard doctrine suggested that Davout would be overrun. Davout's strategy was to refuse the Prussian attack by concentrating artillery fire and small numbers of infantry in depth, then counterattacking against any attempt to break through. For eight hours, Davout maintained this posture against superior Prussian numbers. The Prussian commander, Brunswick, was killed in the fighting. The Prussian assault faltered. By 1600 hours, with reports arriving that French forces had defeated Hohenlohe at Jena and were moving north, the Prussian force at Auerstedt began to retreat. Two separate battles had occurred in the same day on the same campaign. One had been won by Napoleon through local concentration of force. The other had been won by Davout through disciplined defense and concentration of firepower. The strategic result was identical: the Prussian army ceased to exist as a cohesive formation.

The aftermath of October 14 demonstrated the strategic irrelevance of tactical competence when strategic assumptions were false. The Prussian army, which had not been defeated in the field for a century, was shattered in a single day. The retreat was orderly in the initial phases but became a rout as news of failures at both Jena and Auerstedt spread. By October 25, the remnants of the Prussian army, no longer capable of organized resistance, surrendered. The Russian army, which was supposed to coordinate with Prussia, had not reached the theater. The Prussian strategic assumption—that they could hold interior lines until Russian support arrived—became irrelevant after October 14. The Prussian army was no longer present to hold anything.

The Prussian General Staff's assessment of the 1806 campaign, compiled immediately after the war, concluded that the primary failure had been strategic, not tactical. The Prussian army had been tactically competent. Officers executed their orders with skill. The Prussian infantry had been trained and disciplined. The artillery had been effective in the individual engagements. What Prussia had failed to do was understand that the French army of 1806 was a different instrument than it had been in 1792. The French had developed operational doctrine—the ability to move armies rapidly, concentrate force at the decisive point, and sustain operations through logistics rather than territorial support—that Prussian defensive doctrine could not counter. The Prussian assumption that superior discipline could substitute for superior strategy was tested on October 14 and found false.

The strategic lesson of Jena-Auerstedt, obscured by Prussian reluctance to admit strategic failure after the war, was that military capability is not a fixed quantity. The Prussian army in 1806 was arguably the most professionally organized and disciplined force in Europe. What it lacked was operational experience against an enemy that was more dangerous in 1806 than it had been in 1792. This gap—between an army's belief about its capability and its actual capability under new circumstances—was wider at Jena than at any other engagement in the Napoleonic Wars. The result was not merely military defeat but strategic collapse. Prussia, which had entered the war expecting to defeat France within the campaign season, was removed from the conflict by October 25. The war between Prussia and France had lasted seventeen days.

shortForm.title: Rossbach: Deception Against Odds
shortForm.excerpt: On November 5, 1757, Frederick II of Prussia was heavily outnumbered by an Austrian-Saxon coalition army. Rather than retreat, Frederick concealed his army's position, moved at night, and attacked the coalition's flank. The enemy was routed. The victory was based on terrain intelligence and operational deception, not numerical strength.
paragraphs: The strategic situation in Saxony in late 1757 was unfavorable for Frederick II. The Austrian and Saxon armies, combined with French contingents, numbered approximately 80,000 men. Frederick's army numbered 22,000. The standard response to such a disparity in strength would have been retreat, consolidation of forces, and wait for logistics to favor the numerically weaker force. Frederick instead chose to attack. The decision was predicated on a specific intelligence advantage: Frederick's scouts had identified a weakness in the coalition's formation and supply line. The coalition was moving in extended order across difficult terrain, with regiments and batteries separated by 5 to 10 kilometers.

On November 5, 1757, Frederick moved his army at night under cover of darkness and poor visibility. The coalition commander, Marshal Daun, did not believe the Prussian army would risk such movement given its numerical inferiority. The assumption was logical but false. By dawn, Frederick's army had moved to a position south and east of the coalition's main force. The Prussian artillery, massed in defensive positions, opened fire on the coalition's flank. The combination of concentrated fire and the psychological effect of an attack from an unexpected direction broke the coalition's formation. The retreat began almost immediately. The engagement lasted fewer than ninety minutes. Prussian casualties were 300. Coalition casualties were 8,000.

Rossbach is frequently cited as a tactical masterpiece, but the tactical analysis masks the strategic decision that preceded it. The decision to attack when outnumbered by 3 to 1 was not irrational risk-taking but was based on specific intelligence about coalition weakness. The execution—movement at night, concentration of force at a weakly defended sector, reliance on fire superiority rather than manpower—was technically sound. What made the engagement strategically significant was that it destroyed the coalition's cohesion. After Rossbach, the coalition forces fragmented into separate armies that could be defeated individually. The numerical superiority that had seemed decisive on November 4 was irrelevant on November 6.

sources.label: Christopher Duffy, Military Experience in the Age of Reason

onThisDay.headline: Joan of Arc Captured at Compiègne
onThisDay.summary: On May 8, 1429, Joan of Arc was captured by Burgundian forces during a skirmish near the town of Compiègne in northern France. She was sold to the English and died at the stake in 1431. The capture marked the end of the military campaign that had altered the course of the Hundred Years' War.
